Assume the Axiom of Choice as in the finite-dimensional Gaussian and Brownian
interfaces. Let a node represent an interval $[u,u+h]$, where $h>0$, and let
$\Delta W\in\mathbb R^m$ be its already sampled parent increment. Draw a fresh
vector $Z\sim N_m(0,(h/4)I_m)$ independently of the parent and of every
innovation used at another node. Store the two child increments
$$\Delta W_L=\tfrac12\Delta W+Z,\qquad \Delta W_R=\tfrac12\Delta W-Z.$$

For a finite ordered list of $q\in\mathbb N_0$ split requests, each naming an
existing leaf, apply the rule once to each requested leaf and retain every
parent. Process a rejected trial's left child before its right child; if a
child is later refined, draw a new independent innovation for it. Each request
replaces one leaf by two children, so the result is a finite rooted tree with
the sampled increments, interval lengths, and left-to-right order. Never
discard a sampled parent and redraw a replacement for the same interval. The
procedure assigns increments at dyadic tree nodes; it does not by itself
define values at nondyadic times or prove that the node-selection rule is
predictable. In an adaptive run, a finite work budget supplies a finite list
of requests.

The independence assertion for the two children is unconditional before the
parent is revealed. Conditional on a fixed parent, their sum is fixed and their
conditional covariance is $-(h/4)I_m$; they are not conditionally independent.
The exact fixed-depth Brownian increment law is proved separately on the A page.

Assume AC and let $d\ge1$ be finite. For $m\in\mathbb R^d$ and a real symmetric positive semidefinite matrix $\Sigma$, a Borel probability law is denoted $N_d(m,\Sigma)$ when a vector X with that law satisfies $u\cdot X\sim N(u\cdot m,u^T\Sigma u)$ for every $u\in\mathbb R^d$. Such a law exists, has mean m and covariance Sigma, and can be realized as $m+\Sigma^{1/2}Z$ with independent standard-normal coordinates. Singular Sigma is allowed. Uniqueness will be proved in the following characteristic-function lemma.

Assume AC. If $X\sim N_d(m,\Sigma)$, then $$\Phi_X(t):=\mathbb E e^{it\cdot X}=\exp(it\cdot m-t^T\Sigma t/2)\qquad(t\in\mathbb R^d).$$ This transform uniquely determines the law, including singular Sigma.

For real $a,b,t$, $\varphi_{aX+b}(t)=e^{itb}\varphi_X(at)$. For a finite mutually independent family $(X_j)_{j=1}^n$ of real random variables, $\varphi_{\sum_jX_j}(t)=\prod_j\varphi_{X_j}(t)$. The empty sum has characteristic function one.

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: Let $D\sim N_m(0,\ell I_m)$ and let $Z\sim N_m(0,(\ell/4)I_m)$ be independent. Put $L=D/2+Z$ and $R=D/2-Z$. The vector $(L,R)$ is a linear image of the independent jointly Gaussian pair $(D,Z)$, so it is jointly Gaussian. Its means are zero, and direct covariance expansion gives $\operatorname{Cov}(L)=\operatorname{Cov}(R)=\tfrac14\ell I_m+\tfrac14\ell I_m=\tfrac\ell2I_m,$ $\operatorname{Cov}(L,R)=\tfrac14\ell I_m-\tfrac14\ell I_m=0.$ Also $L+R=D$ identically.

The joint Gaussian characteristic function of $(L,R)$ from [F2] has zero cross-covariance blocks by step 1.1, so it factors into the product of the characteristic functions of $N_m(0,(\ell/2)I_m)$ in the two blocks. Uniqueness of the multivariate normal law in [F2] therefore gives independent children with those marginal laws. If one conditions on $D$, the common $D/2$ term is fixed and the remaining terms are $Z$ and $-Z$, so their conditional cross-covariance is $-\operatorname{Cov}(Z)=-(\ell/4)I_m$.

At depth $0$ the assertion is the root law. Suppose the increments at depth $k$ are mutually independent with law $N_m(0,(h/2^k)I_m)$. The fresh innovations at depth $k$ are mutually independent and independent of the entire parent family by the input construction. Therefore the pairs consisting of each parent and its own innovation are mutually independent across the depth-$k$ nodes. For each such pair, step 2.1 gives the unconditional joint law of its two children: they are independent $N_m(0,(h/2^{k+1})I_m)$ vectors. Since child pairs from distinct parents are measurable functions of disjoint independent parent-innovation pairs, those pairs are mutually independent as well. Hence all depth-$(k+1)$ increments are mutually independent with the claimed law.

Finite induction from step 3.1 proves the assertion for every fixed $r$. The case $r=0$ is the root law; every interval has positive length by $h>0$, so zero-length nodes are excluded. Sum consistency holds at each node by step 1.1. The result concerns each fixed finite tree, not a claim that an endpoint-selected random traversal is predictable. AC enters only through [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice. Let $B$ be a standard Brownian motion on a
probability space $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ [[def-brownian-motion]]. First
replace the ambient space by its completion, retaining the notation
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ for this extension. This is supplied by
[[thm-completion-of-a-measure-space]]; AC supplies its countable-choice
hypothesis by [[lem-ac-supplies-sequential-choices-for-probability-constructions]].
The coordinate functions, their laws, and their raw sigma-algebras are unchanged.
Four families are distinguished.

1. **Raw natural filtration.** $\mathcal F^0_t:=\sigma(B_s:0\le s\le t)$ for
   $t\ge0$, and $\mathcal F^0_\infty:=\sigma\bigl(\bigcup_{t\ge0}\mathcal F^0_t\bigr)
   =\sigma(B_s:s\ge0)$. Both sigma-algebras exist by
   [[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]], and
   $(\mathcal F^0_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a continuous-time filtration in the sense of
   [[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]], the smallest one
   to which $B$ is adapted. It contains no completion and no right-continuous
   augmentation.
2. **Raw right limit.** $\mathcal F^0_{t+}:=\bigcap_{u>t}\mathcal F^0_u$ for
   $t\ge0$. At $t=0$ this is the germ sigma-algebra used later on this page;
   the uncountable intersection is the decreasing intersection over the
   rational $u>t$, since $t\mapsto\mathcal F^0_t$ is increasing. No null
   sets are adjoined in this operation.
3. **Ambient null ideal and completed raw filtration.** Let
   $$\mathcal N:=\{M\subseteq\Omega:\text{there is }N_0\in\mathcal F\text{ with }P(N_0)=0\text{ and }M\subseteq N_0\}$$
   be the family of all subsets of ambient $P$-null events. These sets are
   ambient-measurable because the ambient probability space was completed.
   This is a sigma-ideal: for a countable family choose null envelopes using
   AC, then take their union; subsets require the same envelope.
   Nullness follows from
   [[prop-null-sets-form-a-sigma-ideal-in-a-complete-space]]. Put
   $$\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_t:=\sigma\bigl(\mathcal F^0_t\cup\mathcal N\bigr),\qquad t\ge0 .$$
   Each $\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_t$ is a sub-sigma-algebra of $\mathcal F$,
   contains every member of $\mathcal N$, and
   $\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_s\subseteq\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_t$ for
   $s\le t$, so $(\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_t)_{t\ge0}$ is a filtration.
4. **Usual augmentation.** $\mathcal F_t:=\bigcap_{u>t}\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_u$
   for $t\ge0$.

The following facts are part of the definition and are the form in which it is
used later.

(a) $\mathcal F^0_t\subseteq\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_t\subseteq\mathcal F_t$
    for every $t\ge0$, and every $\mathcal F_t$ contains $\mathcal N$.
(b) $(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ is increasing and **right-continuous**: for every
    $t\ge0$,
    $$\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s=\mathcal F_t .$$
    Indeed, if $A\in\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s$, fix $u>t$ and take
    $s=(t+u)/2$. Then $A\in\mathcal F_s\subseteq\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_u$.
    Since $u>t$ was arbitrary, $A\in\mathcal F_t$. Conversely
    $t\le s$ gives $\mathcal F_t\subseteq\mathcal F_s$, because
    $\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0$ is increasing and the intersection defining
    $\mathcal F_t$ ranges over the larger parameter set $\{u>t\}\supseteq\{u>s\}$,
    so $\mathcal F_t\subseteq\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s$.
(c) **Every completed set differs from a raw set by a null set.** Let
    $$\mathcal D_t:=\{A\subseteq\Omega:\text{there is }A_0\in\mathcal F^0_t \text{ and }M\in\mathcal N\text{ with }A\triangle A_0\subseteq M\}.$$
    Then $\mathcal D_t$ is a sigma-algebra containing
    $\mathcal F^0_t\cup\mathcal N$: complementation preserves symmetric
    difference, and, after selecting countably many witnesses by AC,
    $$(\bigcup_k A_k)\triangle(\bigcup_k A_{0,k})\subseteq\bigcup_k(A_k\triangle A_{0,k})\subseteq\bigcup_k M_k\in\mathcal N.$$
    Thus $\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_t\subseteq\mathcal D_t$. Conversely,
    if $A\triangle A_0\subseteq M\in\mathcal N$, then
    $A\triangle A_0\in\mathcal N$, so
    $A=A_0\triangle(A\triangle A_0)\in\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_t$.
    This proves equality, and also ambient measurability of every $A\in\mathcal D_t$.
    In particular, for
    $A\in\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_t$ one has $P(A)=P(A_0)$ for such an $A_0$,
    and $\int_AX\,dP=\int_{A_0}X\,dP$ for every integrable real or complex $X$,
    by [[thm-the-lebesgue-integral-respects-almost-everywhere-equality]]
    applied to $X1_A$ and $X1_{A_0}$. Apply it to indicators for the measure
    equality. If $P(A)=0$, its raw representative $A_0$ is null, so
    $A\subseteq A_0\cup M$ is contained in an ambient null envelope.
    Every subset of $A$ therefore belongs to $\mathcal N$.
    This proves completeness of each $\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_t$.
    It also proves completeness of $\mathcal F_t$: a null member belongs
    to $\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_{t+1}$ and hence all its subsets belong to
    $\mathcal N\subseteq\mathcal F_t$. Thus every ambient null event and
    every one of its subsets belongs already to $\mathcal F_0$; together
    with right-continuity, this is the usual-conditions convention used below.
(d) The four families $\mathcal F^0_t$, $\mathcal F^0_{t+}$,
    $\overline{\mathcal F}{}^0_t$ and $\mathcal F_t$ are kept distinct in every
    statement below. The strong Markov theorem is stated for $(\mathcal F_t)$
    and the deterministic Markov theorems are stated for both $(\mathcal F^0_t)$
    and $(\mathcal F_t)$; the companion examples page carries a counterexample
    showing that $\mathcal F^0_{0+}\ne\mathcal F^0_0$ in the canonical
    realization.

The raw filtration remains raw even though the ambient measure has been
completed; no null set is removed from $\Omega$. Choice is used for the
completion theorem and the countable witnesses above, and is also inherited
from the ambient Brownian construction.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a continuous-time filtration
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

1. A map $\tau:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ (infinite values allowed) is a **stopping
   time** for $(\mathcal F_t)$ when
   $$\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0 .$$
2. For a stopping time $\tau$ its **stopped sigma-algebra** is
   $$\mathcal F_\tau:=\{A\in\mathcal F:A\cap\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t \text{ for every }t\ge0\}.$$

The following facts are used below, and each is a direct set computation.

(a) $\mathcal F_\tau$ is a sigma-algebra: $\emptyset\cap\{\tau\le
    t\}=\emptyset\in\mathcal F_t$; for $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ one has
    $A^c\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus(A\cap\{\tau\le t\})\in\mathcal
    F_t$; and for a sequence $A_n\in\mathcal F_\tau$ the union satisfies
    $\bigl(\bigcup_nA_n\bigr)\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcup_n(A_n\cap\{\tau\le
    t\})\in\mathcal F_t$. All operations are literal, not modulo null sets, and
    no completeness of the filtration is assumed.
(b) If $\tau\equiv t_0<\infty$ is deterministic, then
    $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ is $A$ for $t\ge t_0$ and $\emptyset$ for $t<t_0$, so
    $\mathcal F_\tau=\bigcap_{t\ge t_0}\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t_0}$, where
    the last equality follows because the intersection includes its least
    member $\mathcal F_{t_0}$. If $\tau\equiv\infty$, then every test event
    $\{\tau\le t\}$ is empty and $\mathcal F_\tau=\mathcal F$.
(c) Suppose the filtration is right-continuous. Then $\tau$ is a stopping time
    if and only if $\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t>0$. Indeed
    $$\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\}$$
    (with the terms for $t-\tfrac1n<0$ read as the empty set, since
    $\tau\ge0$), which gives the forward implication; conversely
    $$\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\},$$
    and $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s=\mathcal F_t$ by
    right-continuity together with monotonicity of the filtration.
(d) Under the same right-continuity assumption, for $A\in\mathcal F$ one has
    $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ if and only if $A\cap\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for
    every $t>0$: the forward implication follows from
    $A\cap\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_n(A\cap\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\})$ and the converse
    from $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_n(A\cap\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\})$ together with
    $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\mathcal F_t$.

Because the two versions of each test are interchangeable exactly when the
filtration is right-continuous, the convention is recorded here once: the
Brownian strong Markov theorem is stated for the usual augmentation, which is
right-continuous, and the raw-filtration statements use the non-strict test
directly. No choice principle is used by this definition.

Assume the Axiom of Choice. On a probability space
$(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$, a **continuous-time filtration** is a family
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ of sub-sigma-algebras of $\mathcal F$ such that
$\mathcal F_s\subseteq\mathcal F_t$ whenever $0\le s\le t$. A process
$X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$ is **adapted** when $X_t$ is measurable from
$(\Omega,\mathcal F_t)$ to its state space at every $t$.

For any process of random elements $X=(X_t)_{t\ge0}$, its **natural
filtration** is

$$\mathcal F_t^X=\sigma\!\left(\{X_u^{-1}(C):0\le u\le t,\ C\text{ measurable in the state space of }X_u\}\right).$$

The generated sigma-algebra exists by
[[thm-generated-sigma-algebra-exists-and-is-minimal]]. Its generator families
are nested in $t$, so $(\mathcal F_t^X)_{t\ge0}$ is a filtration; every
$X_t$ is $\mathcal F_t^X$-measurable, and minimality makes this the smallest
filtration to which $X$ is adapted. No completion or right-continuous
augmentation is included.

A real process $M=(M_t)_{t\ge0}$ is an **all-pairs continuous-time
martingale** relative to $(\mathcal F_t)$ when:

1. $M$ is adapted;
2. $E|M_t|<\infty$ for every $t\ge0$; and
3. for every $0\le s\le t$,
   $$E[M_t\mid\mathcal F_s]=M_s\qquad\text{almost surely}.$$

The equality in clause 3 is equality of the almost-everywhere classes in
[[def-conditional-expectation-as-an-ae-class]]. At $s=t$ it is the
known-variable identity. The word “continuous-time” specifies the index set;
it does not assert path continuity. Likewise the definition imposes neither
right continuity nor completeness on the filtration. AC is declared exactly
because the library's conditional-expectation existence theorem uses it; the
filtration, adaptation, and natural-filtration constructions make no choices.

derivations.claim: Fix $t\in(0,T]$ and, for each integer $n\ge1$, form the deterministic grid $G_{n,t}=\{kt2^{-n}:0\le k\le2^n\}$. Let $\tau_{n,t}$ be the least point of $G_{n,t}$ greater than or equal to $\tau\wedge t$. For $s<t$, $\{\tau_{n,t}\le s\}=\bigcup_{q\in G_{n,t},\ q\le s}\{\tau\le q\}\in\mathcal F_s$ by [F2] and [F3]; for $s\ge t$ the event is all of $\Omega$. Thus $\tau_{n,t}$ is a finite-valued stopping time, $\tau_{n,t}\le t$, and $\tau_{n,t}\downarrow\tau\wedge t$. Each event $\{\tau_{n,t}=q\}$ belongs to $\mathcal F_q$ by subtracting consecutive sublevel events, so the finite-valued variable $X_{\tau_{n,t}}$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable by [F3].

Define $Z_t$ as the limit of $X_{\tau_{n,t}}$ where that finite vector limit exists, and as $0$ otherwise. Since each approximant is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable, $Z_t$ is $\mathcal F_t$-measurable. On $\{\tau\le t\}$ and on the full-probability continuity event, $\tau_{n,t}\downarrow\tau$ and continuity gives $Z_t=X_\tau$. The case $t=0$ follows directly from $\tau\wedge0=0$ and $Z_0=X_0$.

For any Borel set $C\subseteq\mathbb R^d$, the events $\{X_\tau\in C\}\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ and $\{Z_t\in C\}\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ differ only on the measurable null set where path continuity may fail. The second event is in $\mathcal F_t$ by [F2] and step 2.1; [F1] places their symmetric difference in $\mathcal F_t$, so the first event is in $\mathcal F_t$. At $t=T$ this also gives $\{X_\tau\in C\}\in\mathcal F_T$. All tests in [F2] hold, proving $X_\tau\in\mathcal F_\tau$. AC enters only through [A1].

Assume AC. Fix $T>0$ and a finite partition $0=t_0<t_1<\cdots<t_N=T$.
Let $W$ be a scalar Brownian motion adapted to $(\mathcal F_t)$, with
$W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and distributed as $N(0,t-s)$ for
every $0\le s<t\le T$. If each $\xi_k$ is real-valued,
$\mathcal F_{t_k}$-measurable and square-integrable, then the predictable
step process
$$H_s=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\xi_k1_{(t_k,t_{k+1}]}(s)$$
is square-integrable. Every continuous version of its Itô integral agrees, at every time on one
measurable event of probability one, with
$$S_t=\sum_{k=0}^{N-1}\xi_k\bigl(W_{t\wedge t_{k+1}}-W_{t\wedge t_k}\bigr),\qquad 0\le t\le T.$$
If the probability space is complete, this agreement is indistinguishability.
The coefficients need not be bounded.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,
$$E\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)^2=E\int_0^TH^2ds=\|H\|^2_{L^2(\mathrm dt\otimes P)},$$
it takes values in the mean-zero subspace of $L^2(P)$, and the bilinear cross
identity
$$E\Bigl[\Bigl(\int_0^TH\,dB\Bigr)\Bigl(\int_0^TK\,dB\Bigr)\Bigr]=E\int_0^TH_sK_s\,ds$$
holds for all such $H,K$. In particular the image of the map is a closed
subspace of $L^2(P)$ isometric to the predictable $L^2$ space of $H$'s, and
$H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is injective up to the $(\mathrm dt\otimes P)$-class.

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let

2. For a stopping time $\tau$ its **stopped sigma-algebra** is
   $$\mathcal F_\tau:=\{A\in\mathcal F:A\cap\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t \text{ for every }t\ge0\}.$$

The following facts are used below, and each is a direct set computation.

(a) $\mathcal F_\tau$ is a sigma-algebra: $\emptyset\cap\{\tau\le
    t\}=\emptyset\in\mathcal F_t$; for $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ one has
    $A^c\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus(A\cap\{\tau\le t\})\in\mathcal

    $\bigl(\bigcup_nA_n\bigr)\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcup_n(A_n\cap\{\tau\le

    no completeness of the filtration is assumed.

    $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ is $A$ for $t\ge t_0$ and $\emptyset$ for $t<t_0$, so
    $\mathcal F_\tau=\bigcap_{t\ge t_0}\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t_0}$, where
    the last equality follows because the intersection includes its least
    member $\mathcal F_{t_0}$. If $\tau\equiv\infty$, then every test event
    $\{\tau\le t\}$ is empty and $\mathcal F_\tau=\mathcal F$.

    if and only if $\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t>0$. Indeed
    $$\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\}$$
    (with the terms for $t-\tfrac1n<0$ read as the empty set, since
    $\tau\ge0$), which gives the forward implication; conversely
    $$\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\},$$
    and $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s=\mathcal F_t$ by

[[alg-euler-maruyama]]. The inputs are $T>0$, the coefficients $b,\sigma$,
the Brownian path or increment source, an initial value $X_0$, a deterministic
maximum step $h_{\max}>0$, and a deterministic work budget
$B\in\mathbb N_0$. Stopped Brownian values are measurable at their stopped
sigma-algebras by [[lem-continuous-adapted-process-at-bounded-stopping-time]],
and each stopping time $\tau_n$ is $\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$-measurable by the
event tests of [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]]. Since $h_n$ is
$\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$-measurable, Borel coefficient evaluation and the
predictable-grid update keep $Y_n$ measurable at $\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$ by
induction. The continuous interpolation is adapted as well: at each fixed
$t$, the active-interval events are in $\mathcal F_t$ by the stopping-time
tests, and each term uses stopped values restricted to $\{\tau_n\le t\}$. Choose
one of the following modes.

1. **Predictable-grid mode.** Supply a finite predictable grid
   [[def-predictable-stopping-time-grid]] with
   $h_n\le h_{\max}$ on every active interval. Initialize $Y_0=X_0$ and
   process its intervals in order until the grid reaches $T$ or the budget
   is exhausted. Each interval uses the actual Brownian increment and update
   $$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(\tau_n,Y_n)h_n+ \sigma(\tau_n,Y_n)(W_{\tau_{n+1}}-W_{\tau_n}).$$
   The continuous interpolation on the interval is
   $$Y_t=Y_n+b(\tau_n,Y_n)(t-\tau_n)+ \sigma(\tau_n,Y_n)(W_t-W_{\tau_n}).$$
   This is the Euler–Maruyama update of [[alg-euler-maruyama]] with the
   supplied interval length; the fixed-grid supplier itself makes no
   variable-grid convergence assertion.

2. **Endpoint-refinement mode.** Supply a total Borel-measurable Boolean-valued
   accept/reject rule on the finite-dimensional current trial data. Initialize a queue with a finite partition
   $0=u_0<\cdots<u_J=T$ whose root intervals have lengths at most
   $h_{\max}$, together with their sampled Brownian increments. Pop the
   earliest interval $[u,u+\ell]$, form the Euler trial
   $Y^*=Y+b(u,Y)\ell+\sigma(u,Y)\Delta W$, and apply the supplied
   accept/reject rule. If accepted, set $Y\leftarrow Y^*$, append the
   right-endpoint/state pair to the accepted path record, and advance to the
   interval's right endpoint. If rejected, retain its parent increment,
   split it with [[alg-dyadic-brownian-bridge-increment-tree]], and put its
   left then right children at the front of the queue; do not update $Y$ on
   the rejected parent and do not redraw the parent or either child. This
   branch preserves the sampled path tree, but an endpoint-dependent
   acceptance rule is not a predictable-grid controller;
   the strong-error theorem on this page makes no error claim for this branch.

`trial_count=0`. Maintain `current_time` and `current_state` as the endpoint
and Euler state of the accepted path. In endpoint-refinement mode, also
initialize the accepted path record with $(0,X_0)$; append each
right-endpoint/state pair only when its interval is accepted.

trial, increment `trial_count` by one. Before the first trial and after every
trial, first check whether the mode's completion condition holds: the supplied
grid has reached $T$ in predictable-grid mode,
or the queue is empty and the accepted path reaches $T$ in endpoint-refinement
mode. If so, return with `status: complete`. Otherwise, if the count has
reached $B$, return with `status: inconclusive`; if not, perform the next
trial. Thus a budget $B=0$ returns `inconclusive`, and a last trial that
reaches $T$ returns `complete`.

trial_count)`. On completion, `current_time=T`, `current_state=Y_T`, and

using information available at its left endpoint. A decision that inspects
$W_{\tau_{n+1}}-W_{\tau_n}$ before fixing $h_n$ is not predictable under this
definition. Brownian-bridge refinement can preserve the sampled path after
such a decision, but does not make that grid predictable.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a locally
square-integrable predictable process
[[def-locally-square-integrable-predictable-brownian-integrand]] with localized
integral $H\cdot B$ in the progressively measurable version of
[[thm-localized-ito-integral]], with its measurable-full-event convention
for indistinguishability. The filtration satisfies the usual conditions and
local energy is finite almost surely on every finite horizon, as required by
the local-integrability definition. Let $\tau$ be a
stopping time [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]]. Then the process
$s\mapsto(H\cdot B)_{s\wedge\tau}$ and the localized integral of the process
$1_{[0,\tau]}H$ are indistinguishable:
$$(H\cdot B)_{t\wedge\tau}=\int_0^t1_{[0,\tau]}(s)H_s\,dB_s\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0\text{, up to indistinguishability}.$$
In particular, for $H$ of finite energy this reduces to the stopping identity
of [[thm-localized-ito-integral]], and for $\tau\equiv\infty$ it is the
definition of the localized integral.

Assume AC and the usual filtered-space hypotheses for the Itô integral. Let
$W$ be a scalar Brownian motion on $[0,T]$, let $0\le\tau\le\sigma\le T$ be
stopping times, and let $\xi\in L^2(\mathcal F_\tau)$. The process
$H_s=\xi\,1_{(\tau,\sigma]}(s)$ is predictable with finite energy, and its
continuous Itô-integral version satisfies
$$\int_0^t H_s\,dW_s=\xi\bigl(W_{t\wedge\sigma}-W_{t\wedge\tau}\bigr) \quad(0\le t\le T)$$
up to indistinguishability. The statement applies coordinatewise to each
entry of a matrix-valued coefficient and a finite-dimensional Brownian motion.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Let $H$ be a predictable
process on $[0,T]$, where $T\ge0$, with $E\int_0^TH_s^2ds<\infty$. Extend $H$ by zero after $T$ when applying the global continuous-version theorem, and let
$M_t=\int_0^tH_s\,dB_s$ be the continuous version of
[[thm-ito-integral-process-has-a-continuous-martingale-version]]. Then
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|M_t|^2\le4\,E\int_0^TH_s^2\,ds .$$
The left-hand side is finite and does not depend on the chosen version, since
any two continuous versions are indistinguishable. Every continuous version of
the integral process satisfies the same bound. The path supremum in this
expectation means its measurable version $S_D=\sup_{q\in D}|M_q|$ on the
countable scaled dyadic grid $D$ (including both endpoints). Continuity
identifies it with the path supremum on a measurable event of probability one.
Indistinguishability here uses that full-event convention, as in the cited
continuous-version theorem, without assuming completeness of the filtration.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2),$$
and
$$|b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}.$$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

Let $t_0\le T$, let $u,a,b:[t_0,T]\to\mathbb R$ be continuous, with $u,b\ge0$, and suppose

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t b(s)u(s)\,ds.$$

Then

$$u(t)\le a(t)+\int_{t_0}^t a(s)b(s)\exp\!\left(\int_s^t b(r)\,dr\right)ds.$$

If $a$ is nondecreasing, this gives $u(t)\le a(t)\exp(\int_{t_0}^t b)$. The time-reflected form assumes $u(t)\le a(t)+\int_t^{t_0}b(s)u(s)\,ds$ for $t\le t_0$. In particular, when $a=A\ge0$ and $b=B\ge0$ are constant, the two orientations give $u(t)\le A e^{B|t-t_0|}$.

Let $(f_n)$ be nonnegative measurable functions. Then
$$\int \liminf_{n\to\infty}f_n\,d\mu\le\liminf_{n\to\infty}\int f_n\,d\mu.$$

Let $(\Omega,\mathcal F,P)$ be a probability space and let
$(\mathcal F_t)_{t\ge0}$ be a continuous-time filtration
[[def-continuous-time-filtration-and-all-pairs-martingale]].

1. A map $\tau:\Omega\to[0,\infty]$ (infinite values allowed) is a **stopping
   time** for $(\mathcal F_t)$ when
   $$\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t\qquad\text{for every }t\ge0 .$$
2. For a stopping time $\tau$ its **stopped sigma-algebra** is
   $$\mathcal F_\tau:=\{A\in\mathcal F:A\cap\{\tau\le t\}\in\mathcal F_t \text{ for every }t\ge0\}.$$

The following facts are used below, and each is a direct set computation.

(a) $\mathcal F_\tau$ is a sigma-algebra: $\emptyset\cap\{\tau\le
    t\}=\emptyset\in\mathcal F_t$; for $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ one has
    $A^c\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\{\tau\le t\}\setminus(A\cap\{\tau\le t\})\in\mathcal
    F_t$; and for a sequence $A_n\in\mathcal F_\tau$ the union satisfies
    $\bigl(\bigcup_nA_n\bigr)\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcup_n(A_n\cap\{\tau\le
    t\})\in\mathcal F_t$. All operations are literal, not modulo null sets, and
    no completeness of the filtration is assumed.
(b) If $\tau\equiv t_0<\infty$ is deterministic, then
    $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}$ is $A$ for $t\ge t_0$ and $\emptyset$ for $t<t_0$, so
    $\mathcal F_\tau=\bigcap_{t\ge t_0}\mathcal F_t=\mathcal F_{t_0}$, where
    the last equality follows because the intersection includes its least
    member $\mathcal F_{t_0}$. If $\tau\equiv\infty$, then every test event
    $\{\tau\le t\}$ is empty and $\mathcal F_\tau=\mathcal F$.
(c) Suppose the filtration is right-continuous. Then $\tau$ is a stopping time
    if and only if $\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for every $t>0$. Indeed
    $$\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_{n\ge1}\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\}$$
    (with the terms for $t-\tfrac1n<0$ read as the empty set, since
    $\tau\ge0$), which gives the forward implication; conversely
    $$\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_{n\ge1}\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\},$$
    and $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\bigcap_{s>t}\mathcal F_s=\mathcal F_t$ by
    right-continuity together with monotonicity of the filtration.
(d) Under the same right-continuity assumption, for $A\in\mathcal F$ one has
    $A\in\mathcal F_\tau$ if and only if $A\cap\{\tau<t\}\in\mathcal F_t$ for
    every $t>0$: the forward implication follows from
    $A\cap\{\tau<t\}=\bigcup_n(A\cap\{\tau\le t-\tfrac1n\})$ and the converse
    from $A\cap\{\tau\le t\}=\bigcap_n(A\cap\{\tau<t+\tfrac1n\})$ together with
    $\bigcap_n\mathcal F_{t+1/n}=\mathcal F_t$.

Because the two versions of each test are interchangeable exactly when the
filtration is right-continuous, the convention is recorded here once: the
Brownian strong Markov theorem is stated for the usual augmentation, which is
right-continuous, and the raw-filtration statements use the non-strict test
directly. No choice principle is used by this definition.

The map $q \mapsto \hat q$ ([[def-real-numbers]]) is an embedding of ordered
fields. Every real is approximated by rationals: for $x \in \mathbb{R}$ and
rational $\varepsilon > 0$ there is $q \in \mathbb{Q}$ with
$|x - \hat q| < \hat\varepsilon$. Consequently, strictly between any two
reals lies a rational.

Let $(X,\mathcal A,\mu)$ be an arbitrary measure space. All functions below have domain $X$. Let $f$ and $(f_n)$ be measurable complex-valued functions such that
$f_n\to f$ almost everywhere and $|f_n|\le g$ almost everywhere for a single
nonnegative measurable function $g$ with $\int g\,d\mu<+\infty$. Then
$f\in L^1(\mu)$,
$$\int|f_n-f|\,d\mu\longrightarrow0,$$
and hence
$$\int f_n\,d\mu\longrightarrow\int f\,d\mu.$$

The **Axiom of Choice** (AC) is the following statement.

> Every family of nonempty sets has a choice function
> ([[def-choice-function]]).

Written out: for every set $\mathcal{F}$ all of whose members are nonempty,
there exists a function $g$ with domain $\mathcal{F}$ satisfying $g(S) \in S$ for
all $S \in \mathcal{F}$.

An equivalent formulation is that a product of nonempty sets is nonempty: if
$X_i \ne \emptyset$ for every $i \in I$, then $\prod_{i \in I} X_i \ne \emptyset$.
Here $\prod_{i \in I} X_i$ is the set of functions $f$ with domain $I$ such that
$f(i) \in X_i$ for every $i \in I$; when a family of nonempty sets is indexed by
itself, such an $f$ is precisely a choice function for it.

derivations.claim: For $R>0$ define $\rho_R=\inf\{t\le T:|Y_t|\ge R\}\wedge T$, taking $\rho_R=T$ if the set is empty. For an integer $k\ge1$, set $\theta_{R,k}=\rho_R\wedge\tau_k$ and $Y^{R,k}_t=Y_{t\wedge\theta_{R,k}}$. Continuity, adaptedness and [F8] make $\rho_R$ a stopping time, so $\theta_{R,k}$ is a stopping time. For the first $k$ intervals, multiply each left-endpoint coefficient by $1_{\{|Y_n|\le |X_0|\vee R\}}$. These factors are measurable at $\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$, the truncated coefficients are in $L^2$ by [F5], and they agree with the original coefficients before $\theta_{R,k}$, except at time endpoints which do not affect the integrals. Thus [F3] gives their finite-step integral representation, to which [F2] applies. Before $\theta_{R,k}$, every active left-endpoint value is bounded by $|X_0|\vee R$; [F5] and $X_0\in L^2$ therefore give finite expected coefficient energy. Applying [F2] at $\theta_{R,k}$ to the finite-step integral representation yields $Y^{R,k}_t=X_0+\int_0^t1_{[0,\theta_{R,k}]}(s)\bar b_s\,ds+\int_0^t1_{[0,\theta_{R,k}]}(s)\bar\sigma_s\,dW_s$, where $\bar b_s=b(\tau_n,Y_n)$ and $\bar\sigma_s=\sigma(\tau_n,Y_n)$ on active intervals. Also $\sup_{u\le t}|Y^{R,k}_u|\le |X_0|\vee R$, so $U_{R,k}(t):=\mathbb E\sup_{u\le t}|Y^{R,k}_u|^2$ is finite and continuous by [F9], since the path suprema converge pointwise with $t$ and are bounded by the integrable variable $(|X_0|\vee R)^2$.

Write each coordinate of the stopped martingale as $M^i=\sum_{j=1}^m M^{ij}$, with $M^{ij}_t=\int_0^t1_{[0,\theta_{R,k}]}(s)\bar\sigma^{ij}_s\,dW^j_s$. For every $i,j$, [F4] applies to the scalar Brownian coordinate $W^j$. The inequalities $\sup_t|\sum_jM^{ij}_t|^2\le m\sum_j\sup_t|M^{ij}_t|^2$ and $|a+b+c|^2\le3(|a|^2+|b|^2+|c|^2)$ give the martingale bound $4m\mathbb E\int_0^t1_{[0,\theta_{R,k}]}\|\bar\sigma_s\|_F^2ds$. Cauchy–Schwarz bounds the squared drift supremum by $T\int_0^t1_{[0,\theta_{R,k}]}|\bar b_s|^2ds$. On an active interval, $|\bar Y_s|^2\le\sup_{u\le s}|Y^{R,k}_u|^2$; using [F5] in the representation of step 1.1 yields $U_{R,k}(t)\le3\mathbb E|X_0|^2+(3T+12m)K^2\int_0^t(1+U_{R,k}(s))ds$.
Apply [F6] to $1+U_{R,k}$ with $A=1+3\mathbb E|X_0|^2$ and $C=(3T+12m)K^2$. Then $U_{R,k}(T)\le(1+3\mathbb E|X_0|^2)e^{(3T+12m)K^2T}-1$, uniformly in $R,k$.

Since $N<\infty$ almost surely, for almost every path $\tau_k=T$ for all sufficiently large $k$. Thus $Y^{R,k}$ eventually equals $Y^{\rho_R}$ uniformly on $[0,T]$; [F7] passes the bound of step 3.1 to $\mathbb E\sup_{t\le T}|Y_{t\wedge\rho_R}|^2$. Each continuous path $Y$ is bounded on $[0,T]$, so $Y^{\rho_R}\to Y$ uniformly almost surely as $R\to\infty$, and [F7] gives the stated bound. The cases $X_0=0$ or $K=0$ are covered by the same inequality, and no lower mesh bound or deterministic bound on $N$ is used. AC is inherited only through [A1].

Assume the Axiom of Choice and use the finite-dimensional Brownian-motion
convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2),$$
and
$$|b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}.$$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

The **Euler–Maruyama algorithm** takes these data as input and returns
$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.

Assume AC and use the coefficient, Brownian, and initial-value conventions of
[[alg-euler-maruyama]]. The inputs are $T>0$, the coefficients $b,\sigma$,
the Brownian path or increment source, an initial value $X_0$, a deterministic
maximum step $h_{\max}>0$, and a deterministic work budget
$B\in\mathbb N_0$. Stopped Brownian values are measurable at their stopped
sigma-algebras by [[lem-continuous-adapted-process-at-bounded-stopping-time]],
and each stopping time $\tau_n$ is $\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$-measurable by the
event tests of [[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]]. Since $h_n$ is
$\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$-measurable, Borel coefficient evaluation and the
predictable-grid update keep $Y_n$ measurable at $\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$ by
induction. The continuous interpolation is adapted as well: at each fixed
$t$, the active-interval events are in $\mathcal F_t$ by the stopping-time
tests, and each term uses stopped values restricted to $\{\tau_n\le t\}$. Choose
one of the following modes.

1. **Predictable-grid mode.** Supply a finite predictable grid
   [[def-predictable-stopping-time-grid]] with
   $h_n\le h_{\max}$ on every active interval. Initialize $Y_0=X_0$ and
   process its intervals in order until the grid reaches $T$ or the budget
   is exhausted. Each interval uses the actual Brownian increment and update
   $$Y_{n+1}=Y_n+b(\tau_n,Y_n)h_n+ \sigma(\tau_n,Y_n)(W_{\tau_{n+1}}-W_{\tau_n}).$$
   The continuous interpolation on the interval is
   $$Y_t=Y_n+b(\tau_n,Y_n)(t-\tau_n)+ \sigma(\tau_n,Y_n)(W_t-W_{\tau_n}).$$
   This is the Euler–Maruyama update of [[alg-euler-maruyama]] with the
   supplied interval length; the fixed-grid supplier itself makes no
   variable-grid convergence assertion.

2. **Endpoint-refinement mode.** Supply a total Borel-measurable Boolean-valued
   accept/reject rule on the finite-dimensional current trial data. Initialize a queue with a finite partition
   $0=u_0<\cdots<u_J=T$ whose root intervals have lengths at most
   $h_{\max}$, together with their sampled Brownian increments. Pop the
   earliest interval $[u,u+\ell]$, form the Euler trial
   $Y^*=Y+b(u,Y)\ell+\sigma(u,Y)\Delta W$, and apply the supplied
   accept/reject rule. If accepted, set $Y\leftarrow Y^*$, append the
   right-endpoint/state pair to the accepted path record, and advance to the
   interval's right endpoint. If rejected, retain its parent increment,
   split it with [[alg-dyadic-brownian-bridge-increment-tree]], and put its
   left then right children at the front of the queue; do not update $Y$ on
   the rejected parent and do not redraw the parent or either child. This
   branch preserves the sampled path tree, but an endpoint-dependent
   acceptance rule is not a predictable-grid controller;
   the strong-error theorem on this page makes no error claim for this branch.

For either mode, initialize `current_time=0`, `current_state=X_0`, and
`trial_count=0`. Maintain `current_time` and `current_state` as the endpoint
and Euler state of the accepted path. In endpoint-refinement mode, also
initialize the accepted path record with $(0,X_0)$; append each
right-endpoint/state pair only when its interval is accepted.
Count every trial node, accepted or rejected, as one work unit; after each
trial, increment `trial_count` by one. Before the first trial and after every
trial, first check whether the mode's completion condition holds: the supplied
grid has reached $T$ in predictable-grid mode,
or the queue is empty and the accepted path reaches $T$ in endpoint-refinement
mode. If so, return with `status: complete`. Otherwise, if the count has
reached $B$, return with `status: inconclusive`; if not, perform the next
trial. Thus a budget $B=0$ returns `inconclusive`, and a last trial that
reaches $T$ returns `complete`.

Both statuses use the output record
`(mode, status, current_time, current_state, approximation, pending_work,
trial_count)`. On completion, `current_time=T`, `current_state=Y_T`, and
`pending_work` is empty. The `approximation` is the full continuous Euler
interpolation in predictable-grid mode; in endpoint-refinement mode it is the
accepted ordered endpoint/state record together with the retained increment
tree. On an inconclusive return, `trial_count=B`, `current_state` is the state
at `current_time`, and `approximation` is the partial output through that
time: the continuous interpolation restricted to $[0,\texttt{current\_time}]$
in predictable-grid mode, and the accepted endpoint/state record and retained
tree in endpoint-refinement mode. `pending_work` is the remaining ordered grid
suffix or the current ordered tree queue, respectively. The tree assigns no
values at non-dyadic times, so endpoint-refinement mode returns its accepted
node record rather than a continuous interpolation. A finite budget never
changes an inconclusive result into a successful certificate.

Assume $T>0$ and work on a filtered probability space with stopping times and
stopped sigma-algebras as defined in
[[def-continuous-time-stopping-time]]. A **finite predictable stopping-time
grid** on $[0,T]$ is a random integer $N<\infty$ almost surely and a sequence
of stopping times
$$0=\tau_0<\tau_1<\cdots<\tau_N=T$$
such that, for each $n<N$, the step length
$h_n=\tau_{n+1}-\tau_n$ is $\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$-measurable and satisfies
$0<h_n\le h_{\max}$ for a deterministic $h_{\max}>0$. Extend the sequence by
$\tau_n=T$ and $h_n=0$ for $n\ge N$. A **budgeted** predictable grid has a
deterministic integer $B$ with $N\le B$ almost surely.

The condition $h_n\in\mathcal F_{\tau_n}$ says the next interval is selected
using information available at its left endpoint. A decision that inspects
$W_{\tau_{n+1}}-W_{\tau_n}$ before fixing $h_n$ is not predictable under this
definition. Brownian-bridge refinement can preserve the sampled path after
such a decision, but does not make that grid predictable.

Work on a filtered probability space satisfying the usual conditions for the
It\^o integral. Assume the coefficient and Brownian hypotheses of
[[alg-euler-maruyama]] on $[0,T]$: finite state/noise dimensions, a square
integrable $\mathcal F_0$-measurable initial value, globally Lipschitz state
dependence, linear growth, and the stated half-Hölder time modulus. Let a
finite predictable grid as in
[[def-predictable-stopping-time-grid]] have $N<\infty$ almost surely and
maximum step at most $h_{\max}\le T$. Form the complete continuous Euler
interpolation by applying the predictable-grid updates in
[[alg-adaptive-euler-maruyama-on-predictable-grid]] on every interval. A
finite-budget execution returns this interpolation as complete when its
budget $B$ satisfies $N\le B$. Then a finite constant
$C=C(T,K,m,\mathbb E|X_0|^2)$ satisfies
$$\mathbb E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|Y_t|^2\le C.$$
The bound is uniform over the controller and the number and placement of its
predictable steps; no deterministic bound on $N$ is needed for this moment
estimate.

Assume AC and the usual filtered-space hypotheses for the Itô integral. Let
$W$ be a scalar Brownian motion on $[0,T]$, let $0\le\tau\le\sigma\le T$ be
stopping times, and let $\xi\in L^2(\mathcal F_\tau)$. The process
$H_s=\xi\,1_{(\tau,\sigma]}(s)$ is predictable with finite energy, and its
continuous Itô-integral version satisfies
$$\int_0^t H_s\,dW_s=\xi\bigl(W_{t\wedge\sigma}-W_{t\wedge\tau}\bigr) \quad(0\le t\le T)$$
up to indistinguishability. The statement applies coordinatewise to each
entry of a matrix-valued coefficient and a finite-dimensional Brownian motion.

Assume the data and hypotheses of
[[def-ito-sde-and-strong-solution]] on $[0,T]$, with $T\ge0$, finite
dimensions $d,m\ge1$, Lipschitz constant $L$, and linear-growth constant
$K$. There is a strong solution $X$ on the given filtered probability space.
It is unique up to indistinguishability among strong solutions with the same
initial value and Brownian driver, and it satisfies
$$E\sup_{0\le t\le T}|X_t|^2\le(1+3E|X_0|^2)e^{C_TT},\qquad C_T:=6K^2T+24mK^2.$$
The bound is independent of any later numerical mesh.

Assume the Axiom of Choice and the standing hypothesis (H) of
[[def-elementary-predictable-brownian-integrand]]. Fix $T>0$. For predictable
$H,K$ with finite energy $E\int_0^TH^2ds,E\int_0^TK^2ds<\infty$ the integrals
$\int_0^TH\,dB$ of
[[def-ito-integral-for-square-integrable-predictable-processes]] satisfy
$$\int_0^T(H+K)\,dB=\int_0^TH\,dB+\int_0^TK\,dB,\qquad \int_0^T(aH)\,dB=a\int_0^TH\,dB\quad(a\in\mathbb R),$$
and the identities are equalities of $L^2(P)$-classes (almost sure
equalities). Moreover the map $H\mapsto\int_0^TH\,dB$ is an isometry,

convention of [[def-d-dimensional-brownian-motion]]. Let the state dimension
$d$ and noise dimension $m$ be positive finite integers, and fix $T>0$ and
$N\in\mathbb N$ with $N\ge1$. Set $h=T/N>0$ and $t_k=kh$ for
$0\le k\le N$. Let
$b:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^d$ and
$\sigma:[0,T]\times\mathbb R^d\to\mathbb R^{d\times m}$ be jointly Borel.
Write $|\cdot|$ for the Euclidean norm and $\|\cdot\|_F$ for the Frobenius
norm. Suppose finite constants $L,K$ satisfy, for every $s,t\in[0,T]$ and
$x,y\in\mathbb R^d$,
$$|b(t,x)-b(t,y)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(t,y)\|_F\le L|x-y|,$$
$$|b(t,x)|^2+\|\sigma(t,x)\|_F^2\le K^2(1+|x|^2),$$
and
$$|b(t,x)-b(s,x)|+\|\sigma(t,x)-\sigma(s,x)\|_F\le K(1+|x|)|t-s|^{1/2}.$$
Let $W$ be an adapted standard $m$-dimensional Brownian motion on a filtered
probability space, with $W_t-W_s$ independent of $\mathcal F_s$ and law
$N_m(0,(t-s)I_m)$ whenever $0\le s<t\le T$. Let $X_0$ be
$\mathcal F_0$-measurable, independent of future Brownian increments, and
$\mathbb E|X_0|^2<\infty$.

$Y_0,\ldots,Y_N$:

1. Set $Y_0=X_0$.
2. For $k=0,\ldots,N-1$, form $\Delta W_k=W_{t_{k+1}}-W_{t_k}$ and set
   $$Y_{k+1}=Y_k+b(t_k,Y_k)h+\sigma(t_k,Y_k)\Delta W_k.$$

The output is the grid approximation for the coefficient pair $(b,\sigma)$.
The companion step-process and interpolation definition uses this same grid
and endpoint convention.
